elements.name: Database platform
elements.description: Control plane owns routing and placement. Data plane consults it and forwards to VM agents.

elements.name: Customer administrator
elements.description: Creates tenants and databases, inspects state and requests database lifecycle operations.

elements.name: Customer query client
elements.description: One session can address any authorized database of its tenant by name or ID through the same query endpoint.

elements.name: Database backup store
elements.description: Verified snapshots per database ID and generation; a backup counts only once its manifest is recorded (M6). Optional WAL frames are future work.

elements.name: Control plane
elements.description: Own routing, registry and VM placement decisions; instruct VM agents for all tenant-file work.

elements.name: Data plane
elements.description: One query endpoint. Obtain a route grant once per grant lifetime, forward with the grant, return results.

elements.name: Postgres metadata
elements.description: Tenants, databases, placement epochs and durable operations. Hand-written SQL; no ORM.

elements.name: VM agent (process)
elements.description: Sole VM tenant-file boundary. Execute queries and lifecycle instructions; report health, size and usage.

elements.name: Statement lanes
elements.description: Private agent-managed execution workers; the lane view (M3) shows their internals. Landed FFI code inside proposed lanes.

elements.name: Database SQLite files
elements.description: One file and WAL/SHM set per database. Separate transactions and writer locks.

elements.name: Management ingress
elements.description: Authenticate administrators. Check permissions. Record idempotent operations and return status.

elements.name: Tenant registry
elements.description: Create, configure and inspect tenants. Drop only after all owned databases are deleted.

elements.name: Database registry
elements.description: Tenant-scoped database CRUD, configure and inspect. Immutable IDs; names are not paths.

elements.name: Database provisioner
elements.description: Choose VM (placement policy OPEN; candidate v1 rule pending Nick's decision, M8). Instruct agent to provision; register placement after confirmation.

elements.name: Database lifecycle
elements.description: Move, suspend/resume, backup/restore, delete and attested recover-from-loss (M5). Fence and drain before changing ownership.

elements.name: Query ingress
elements.description: Select a database by name, or none for `default`, through the same endpoint and session; return results.

elements.name: Session + database auth
elements.description: Derive trusted tenant identity. Resolve the selected (or default) database; verify ownership and grants; stamp database_id into the IR.

elements.name: Control-plane routing
elements.description: Authority for (tenant, database) → VM / epoch. Issues 30 s route grants; out of the per-request path while a grant is valid.
plannedNotes: Tenant-only seam is landed; control-plane database routing (resolve(databaseId), M4), route grants (M1) and remote execution are planned.

elements.name: Owner-node forwarder
elements.description: Forward trusted IDs, grant epoch/generation, request ID, operation IR, SQL/binds and deadline. Invalidate the grant on WrongOwner.

elements.name: VM agent (process) — admission
elements.description: Check database state/epoch per request. Gate, drain and close handles before acknowledging a fence.

elements.name: Statement classifier
elements.description: Landed operation-IR classifier: bounded blocking path or unbounded nonblocking read.

elements.name: FFI statement executor
elements.description: Landed scoped libsqlite3 execution. Reused in proposed lanes; no separate library container.

elements.name: Deadline / interrupt
elements.description: Landed interrupt and settlement. Lane watchdog escalation and database-drain integration are proposed.
plannedNotes: Lane watchdog escalation and database-scoped drain acknowledgement are proposed.

elements.name: Route grant cache
elements.description: Holds route grants per (gateway, database ID): owner VM, epoch, generation, grant version, TTL. Reused until expiry, WrongOwner or revocation; never a lease.

elements.name: Lane IPC endpoint
elements.description: Receives admitted statements from the agent: trusted operation IR, parameterized SQL/binds, database ID, grant epoch, deadline, request ID; returns results, cancels and health.

elements.name: Write-first scheduler + bounded statement pool
elements.description: Semaphore(1) per database file: a mutation waits only on its own file's writer lock, never on read permits. Bounded permit pool for nonblocking steps with a per-database sub-cap; an over-cap database gets a typed QueueFull for itself only.
plannedNotes: Semaphore(1) per file and WRITER_QUEUE_CAP are landed in platform/sqlite.ts; the per-database sub-cap, the write-first rule inside a lane process, tenant-affine assignment, pinning and typed QueueFull are proposed.
elements.technology: Effect Semaphore(1) per file (landed); permit pool (proposed)

elements.name: Handle LRU / read pool
elements.description: One writer handle per database and pooled read-only handles, leased, idle-evicted after transactions settle; accounted at 3 descriptors per writer and 2 per read handle against the VM's nofile capacity.
plannedNotes: The 64-entry leased handle cache with 60 s idle expiry is landed in platform/sqlite.ts; pooled read-only handles per database and descriptor accounting are proposed.
elements.technology: Leased handle cache (landed 64-entry, 60 s idle); per-database read pool (proposed)

elements.name: Request-ID store
elements.description: Request ID and outcome written inside the mutation's own transaction in the database file; looked up before any retry; travels with the database on move and restore. Blind replay is forbidden.
elements.technology: SQLite table in the database file

elements.name: Read-only snapshot connection
elements.description: Backups snapshot through a separate read-only connection (VACUUM INTO), so a backup never holds the writer lock; today Storage.snapshot runs on the writer's queue. quick_check and SHA-256 run on the copy (M6).

elements.name: Backup manifest registry
elements.description: Records backup manifests keyed by (database ID, generation): object key, checksum, format, completion state. Only a recorded manifest is a restore candidate.
elements.technology: Proposed registry logic; Postgres hand-written SQL

elements.name: Platform operator (human)
elements.description: Operates the fleet; attests that a lost VM is isolated before any recovery activates a copy elsewhere. Distinct from the customer administrator.

elements.name: Cloud provider API
elements.description: Answers whether a VM is powered off or network-detached; its recorded response is the proof behind an isolation attestation. A provider dependency this revision accepts.

elements.name: Candidate placement policy v1 (proposed, pending decision)
elements.description: Among eligible VMs pick the lowest descriptor-weighted load: capacity nofile − reserve; 3 descriptors per writer, 2 per pooled reader; size tiebreak. PENDING NICK'S DECISION.

documents.title: Database platform
documents.plain:
Management uses the control plane. Queries use the data plane. Both address databases by tenant and database identity; clients never select a hosting node.

A tenant owns zero or more databases (0..N). The database is the unit of placement, isolation, backup and lifecycle. One-file-per-tenant is superseded in this proposal; the lanes dataset stays unchanged.

The control plane owns routing logic and the placement registry: (tenant, database) resolves to a hosting VM and epoch. The data plane holds a time-boxed route grant from that authority (M1) and reuses it until TTL, WrongOwner or revocation; agent admission rejects stale epochs, which is what makes a stale grant harmless. The topology is n SQLite files across m VMs, not one VM per database or tenant. Placement is a control-plane decision, but how it selects a VM is an OPEN QUESTION: no placement policy or balancing algorithm is solved here. Creation records active placement only after the selected VM agent confirms provisioning; the registry is then the source of truth.

Every hosting VM runs a daemon labelled VM agent (process), software, not AI. It is the sole last-mile tenant-file access boundary on that VM. Outside services never access its disk. Its private managed statement-lane workers execute only behind this agent boundary; they expose no independent file or RPC authority. On instruction the agent executes queries and returns results, provisions, opens/closes, suspends/resumes, snapshots/backs up, copies out/receives moves, restores and deletes files, and reports health, size and usage to the control plane.

Fable revision (DP-02): the planes proposal with modifications M1–M8 from docs/architecture/scale-out-comparison-fable.md applied. Everything an M-number does not name is carried over from tsdb-planes-proposal unchanged. This is a proposal, not landed behavior.

ste.text:
Use the control plane to manage databases. Use the data plane to query a database. The service selects its node.

A tenant can have zero or more databases. Place, isolate, back up and manage each database separately. This proposal replaces one file for each tenant with one file for each database. The lanes dataset does not change.

A lifecycle operation recover-from-loss(vm) has a hard precondition: a platform operator attests the VM is isolated, backed by a provider-level proof (the VM is powered off or its network is detached through the provider API), and the control plane records that response. Then, per database the VM hosted: CAS the placement to FENCED-BY-OPERATOR at a fresh epoch, run the existing restore flow from the latest recorded backup manifest (M6) onto an eligible VM as a fenced generation swap, and activate. Recovery point is the backup interval, stated as such. Without the attestation the operation is refused and the databases stay unavailable: inability to contact the old writer is never permission to activate a copy. This is explicitly not automatic failover. For a drop whose hosting agent is permanently lost, the control plane's lifecycle identity deletes the backup-store objects itself (the store is not VM-local, so the agent-only rule does not apply to it), and the local files are recorded as destroyed with the attested VM. If the old VM ever returns, its files are garbage at a dead epoch and the generation-scoped cleanup rule removes them.

documents.title: Suspend, resume, backup and restore
documents.plain:
Suspend uses the same per-database gate and drain as move; SUSPENDED blocks opens and existing-session admissions. Resume requires verified file readiness, ACTIVE state and a fresh epoch. Backup takes a consistent per-database SQLite backup on a read-only snapshot connection, off the writer lock (M3), and completes only when its manifest is recorded (M6); it does not copy a live main file alone. Operations use durable IDs and state transitions, never a distributed transaction across SQL and files. terms.definition: A time-boxed, revocable record the control-plane routing authority issues to a gateway for one database: owner VM, epoch, generation, grant version and TTL. The gateway reuses it across requests until it expires, WrongOwner invalidates it or a grant-version bump revokes it (M1).
The reserved database named default that every tenant has; a request that names no database gets it. Each existing tenant file becomes its tenant's default database at migration (M4).
The recorded completion record of one backup, keyed by (database ID, generation): object key, checksum, format and completion state. Only a recorded manifest makes a backup a restore candidate (M6).

A platform operator's statement, backed by a recorded provider-API response, that a lost VM is powered off or network-detached. It is the precondition for activating any copy of a database the VM hosted (M5).
